newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia seeks to reduce trade deficit with U.S..
newsitem.headline: Australia seeks to reduce trade deficit with U.S..

text.p: Australia will try to reduce barriers blocking access to U.S. markets in an effort to even out the country's largest bilateral trade imbalance, deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer said on Tuesday.

Fischer, who is also Trade Minister, said he would hold further talks with U.S. Trade Representative-designate Charlene Barshefsky this year, although he said some progress had been made on access barriers.
"We remain concerned about the Export Enhancement Programme for grain subsidisation and the DEIP (Dairy Export Incentive) programme," he told Reuters Financial Television.
"There are still areas of great difficulty which we will continue to negotiate on."
Fischer said Asia remained Australia's top priority for foreign affairs and trade following last year's change of government to a Liberal-National Party coalition.
"(But) it's not a case of Asia full stop. It's a case of Asia and the rest of the world," he said.
Australia enjoyed a trade surplus with Asia as a regional grouping, but had its "worst" trade imbalance with the United States.
Australia recorded a deficit in its merchandise trade balance with the United States in 1995/96 (July-June) of A$12.97 billion (US$10.1 billion).
"There are cyclical and other structural reasons associated with that, but I am not happy about it and we would want to further expand our export effort to the U.S.," Fischer said.
The imbalance would level out rapidly without trade barriers, he said, adding that the Australian and U.S. governments enjoyed a particularly good bilateral relationship.
"I do not see insurmountable problems, but it is the speed at which some of these problems are addressed which is always very pertinent, very relevant," he said.

Fischer also announced on Tuesday that Australia would join New Zealand, Argentina and the United States in taking action in the World Trade Organisation (WTO) against Hungary over agricultural export subsidies.
The move was part of steps by Australia to use the WTO's dispute settlement process more actively to challenge unfair barriers to exports, he said.

Commenting on independent politician Pauline Hanson, who has created controversy by calling for cuts to Asian immigration to Australia, to foreign aid and to welfare for Aborigines, Fischer said he respected her right to speak out.
But he stressed that the Australian government and parliament supported the building of trade, investment and tourism links with Asia, as well as a non-discriminatory immigration policy.
